text:
British Perspective (One of the Big Four)  
 
Maintaining the unity of the British Empire, its holdings, and its interests, were the largest 
concerns of the British delegation. However, their specific goals (in this order) included 
ensuring the security of France, removing the threat of the German High Seas Fleet, settling 
territorial disputes, and demanding and supporting Wilson’s League of Nations. Britain also 
believed that Germany should be made to pay for the war through reparations. At the same 
time, they believed that Germany should be rehabilitated as soon as possible to stabilize 
international trade. Germany was one of the most industrialized nations in the world and, as 
such, was not only an exporter, but a great importer of British materials and goods. Britain 
needed German trade for both economic and political reasons and wished to demand 
economic reparations from Germany. Although you recognize the contributions and sacrifices 
of Indian soldiers, petitions for Indian self-rule will not be up for discussion at this meeting 
since they are the “Crown of the Jewel.” David Lloyd George, the Prime Minister, claimed 
that he did not do badly at the peace conference, “considering I was seated between Jesus 
Christ and Napoleon.” This was a reference to the very idealistic views of Woodrow Wilson 
(US President) and George Clemenceau (France), who were determined to see Germany 
punished. 
 
HINTS:  
1.​ Use statistics to emphasize how much your citizenry lost during the war (these 
statistics include both those from the UK, as well as from their colonies).   
a.​ Civilian casualties included almost 17,000 from military action, another 
100,000 from hunger and disease and another 225,000 from the Influenza 
pandemic.   
b.​ 1.5 million British soldiers were injured.   
c.​ 250,000 British Soldiers suffered a partial or full amputation as a result of 
fighting in the First World War. 
d.​ 744,000 military deaths 
e.​ Almost 2.5% of the total population died (over 1 million people) .  
f.​ (NOTE: THE COUNTRY WITH THE MOST MILITARY DEATHS WAS 
GERMANY—2 million)  
2.​ Show no mercy to Germany.

text:
French Approach (One of the Big Four) 
 
Between 1914 and 1918, 7.9 million French citizens were called to serve in the armed forces.  
In addition to these, 600,000 more soldiers from the colonies (who were not French citizens), 
enlisted in the army and about 500,000 saw combat in Europe. Over 4.2 million soldiers were 
wounded, over 500,000 were taken prisoner and roughly 1.4 million were killed. Afterwards, 
during the Paris Peace Conference, the French Prime Minister, George Clemenceau’s chief 
goal was to weaken Germany militarily, strategically, and economically. Having personally 
witnessed two German attacks on French soil in the previous forty years, he was adamant that 
Germany should not be permitted to attack France again. In particular, Clemenceau sought an 
American and British guarantee of French security in the event of another German attack. 
Clemenceau also expressed skepticism and frustration with Wilson’s Fourteen Points: “Mr. 
Wilson bores me with his fourteen points,” complained Clemenceau. “Why, God Almighty 
has only ten!” Wilson did sign a mutual defense treaty with France, but back in Washington, 
the Senate refused to ratify it. Another alternative French policy was to seek a rapprochement 
[an establishment or resumption of harmonious relations] with Germany.  
 
In May 1919 the diplomat Rene Massigli was sent on several secret missions to Berlin. 
During his visits, Massigli offered on behalf of his government to revise the territorial and 
economic clauses of the upcoming peace treaty. Massigli told the Germans that the French 
thought of the “Anglo-Saxon powers,” namely the US and the British empire as a major 
threat to France in the post-war world. He argued that both France and Germany had a joint 
interest in opposing “Anglo-Saxon” domination of the world and warned that the “deepening 
of opposition” between the French and the Germans “would lead to the ruin of both countries, 
to the advantage of the Anglo-Saxon powers.” The Germans rejected the French offers 
because they considered the French overtures to be a trap to trick them into accepting the 
Versailles treaty “as is” and because the Germans thought the US was more likely to reduce 
the severity of the peace terms than France.  In the end, it was the British who eased up 
slightly on the terms. 
 
HINTS:  
1.​ You want to emphasize how much you lost in terms of farmland, population, military 
and industrial capacity. Somebody must pay for your loss in global status, economic 
strength, and manpower.  
2.​ You want to negotiate for anything that will weaken Germany—especially the 
German war machine.  They have invaded you twice in the past forty years, and you 
want to cripple their ability to do so again—that means industrially (remember they 
have overtaken you in recent years as an industrial superpower) and militarily 
(especially their navy).

text:
Italian Approach (One of the Big Four) 
 
In 1882 Italy joined the German Empire and the Austro-Hungarian empire forming the Triple 
Alliance.  During World War I, Italy aligned itself with the Allies, instead of joining its allies 
in the Triple Alliance.  In the Treaty of London in 1915, Britain and France promised Italy a 
great deal of territory that had been part of the Austro-Hungarian empire, including parts 
north of Italy, much of the Balkans, and a share of Turkish and German empires in Africa. 
Vittorio Orlando was sent as the Italian representative with the aim of gaining these and as 
much other territory as possible. The loss of 700,000 Italians and a budget deficit of 12 
trillion Lire during the war made the Italian government and people feel entitled to these 
territories.  By the end of the war, the Allies had made contradictory agreements with other 
nations, especially in Central Europe and the Middle East. In meetings of the Big Four, 
Orlando’s diplomatic skills were hampered by his lack of English. While Italy did get 
Trentino to the Brenner, the Dalmatian port of Zara, the Island of Lagosta, and a couple of 
small German colonies. All other territories were promised to other nations since the great 
powers were worried about Italy's imperial ambitions. As a result of this, Orlando left the 
conference in a rage. 
 
HINTS: 
1.​ How did the Italians lose so many men?   
2.​ What was significant about the Treaty of London? 
3.​ What was the role of Italy in the drafting of the League of Nations covenant?   
4.​ You may have to storm out of the Paris Peace Conference at some point.  
​

text:
American Approach (One of the Big Four) 
 
President Woodrow Wilson’s 14 Points helped to convince many in the world that a real 
peace was possible, especially Americans, Germans, and other Europeans, as well as the 
former subjects of the Ottoman Empire. Wilson’s diplomacy and his vision for the future had 
set the conditions for the armistice that had ended the Great War. Wilson thought it was his 
duty and obligation to the people of the world to be at the negotiations (leaving the US as 
President for six months!).  He tried to lead the United States towards a policy of 
interventionism—a move strongly resisted by some Americans back home who preferred to 
isolate the United States from further involvement in global conflict.  Wilson worked to 
convince the French and the British delegations that peace would best be served by a less 
harsh treatment of Germany and its allies in Europe, as well as on what should be done with 
the Ottoman lands in the Middle East. He was not able to get many of his 14 points passed 
since France and Britain refused to compromise on the War Guilt clause (Article 231) 
whereas the United States did not encourage nor believe that the responsibility for the war 
placed on Germany was fair or warranted. It would not be until 1921 that the United States 
finally signed separate peace treaties with Germany, Austria, and Hungary. In the Middle 
East, negotiations were complicated by competing aims, claims, and the new mandate 
system.  
 
The United States hoped to establish a more liberal and diplomatic world, where democracy, 
sovereignty, liberty, and self-determination would be respected. France and Britain, on the 
other hand, already controlled empires, and wished to remain dominant colonial powers.  In 
light of the previously secret Sykes-Picot agreement, and following the adoption of the 
mandate system on the Arab province of the former Ottoman lands, the conference heard 
statements from competing Zionist and Arab claimants. President Woodrow Wilson then 
recommended an international commission of inquiry to ascertain the wishes of the local 
inhabitants. This was rejected by the French and the British, paving the way for the formation 
of a Zionist homeland in Palestine, what would later be Israel. France and Britain tried to 
appease the American President by consenting to the establishment of his League of Nations. 
However, because isolationist sentiment was strong and some of the articles in the League’s 
charter conflicted with the US Constitution, the US never did ratify the Treaty of Versailles, 
nor join the League of Nations, which President Wilson had helped create, to further peace 
through diplomacy rather than war and conditions which can breed it. 
 
HINTS: 
1.​ Know the 14 points and which ones were not accepted at the Peace Conference  
2.​ Understand what self-determination means to President Wilson, and what it means to 
small nations in Europe, Asia and Africa  
3.​ Why was it believed that the League of Nations could preserve the peace?

text:
Japanese Approach 
 
The Japanese delegation was headed by Marquess Saionji Kinmochi, Baron Makino 
Nobuaki, and 62 others, making a total of 64.  The delegation focused on two demands: the 
inclusion of their racial equality proposal in the League’s Covenant and Japanese territorial 
claims with respect to former German colonies, namely Shan Tung, and the Pacific Islands 
north of the Equator (the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, the Mariana Islands, and the 
Carolines.) The Japanese claim to Shan Tung was disputed by the Chinese. In 1914, at the 
outset of the war, Japan had seized the territory granted to Germany in 1897.  Secret 
agreements with the Allies led to an eventual resolution in Japan’s favor, leading to Article 
156 of the Treaty of Versailles which transferred German concessions in Kiaochow, China to 
Japan rather than returning sovereignty to China.   
 
This would later lead to the May Fourth Movement. The Japanese delegation still became 
unhappy after receiving only one-half of the rights of Germany and walked out of the 
conference.   Japan proposed including a “racial equality clause” in the Covenant of the 
League of Nations on February 13 as an amendment to Article 21: “The equality of nations 
being a basic principle of the League of Nations, the High Contracting Parties, agree to 
accord as soon as possible to all alien nationals of states, members of the League, equal and 
just treatment in every respect-making no distinction, either in law or in fact, on account of 
their race or nationality.“ Because he knew that Great Britain was critical to the decision, 
President Wilson, as Conference chairman, ruled that a unanimous vote was required. 
However, the Australians had convinced Great Britain to also vote against it. The defeat of 
the proposal influenced Japan’s turn from cooperation with the West to more militant 
nationalism 
 
HINTS:  
1.​ The Japanese were great diplomats in Paris, definitely turning what seemed like 
pro-Chinese feelings by the west into pro-Japanese decisions.  Be sure you know how 
they did this?  What was the deal with those secret treaties? 
2.​  Japan wanted to be considered a major power by the West.  Their loss of face in not 
gaining as much territory as they wanted (resources are important to fuel the growing 
industrial economy), as well as the humiliation they faced at the hands of Australia 
(and the UK) when they refused the Racial Equality Clause is important to 
understand.

text:
Chinese Perspective 
 
At the time of the Paris Peace Conference, there were two governments claiming to be the 
legitimate government of China: the Beiyang government in Beijing, and Dr Sun Yat-Sen’s 
Guangzhou based Kuomintang (KMT) movement. However, they worked together to create 
the united diplomatic team that would plead China’s case in Paris. In January 1915, Japan 
presented a list of demands to Chinese President Yuan Shih-k’ai, known as the “Twenty-one 
Demands,” seeking to assert and expand Japanese control over various regions of China that 
the country had interest in.  
 
Among these regions was Shandong Province, a stipulation that garnered much opposition 
within China,  Chief delegate and Foreign Minister Lu Cheng-hsiang, who had signed one of 
the treaties resulting from the Twenty-one Demands, headed the Chinese delegation. Students 
and others opposed to Japanese expansionist policies saw him as a worrisome addition to the 
delegation given that Chinese territoriality was being called into question at the peace talks 
with the Shandong Province issue. Also, in the delegation were Wellington Koo and Cao 
Rulin.  Koo demanded that Japan return Shandong to China.  He further called for an end to 
imperialist institutions such as extraterritoriality, legation guards, and foreign leaseholds.  
Despite American support, and his proclamations of self-determination, the western powers 
refused his claims.  Inspired by Wilsonian rhetoric like the Fourteen Points Speech, 
nationalists in colonial and semi-colonial countries such as China launched campaigns to 
demand self-determination and international equality.  However, public opinion in general 
seemed to be in accord with the peace talks. Then, in late April, word came that control of 
Shandong, formerly held by Germany, would be accorded to Japan and not China. Going 
directly against the sentiment of national unity, this development acted as a catalyst for the 
student organizations that firmly opposed the move. Thus, the Chinese delegation at the Paris 
Peace Conference was the only one not to sign the Treaty of Versailles at the final ceremony.  
 
HINTS: 
1.​ How did the lack of a unified government in China at the time influence the success 
of the talks?  
2.​ Why didn’t the Americans back the Chinese, as promised, in the final decision to 
grant Japan, Chinese territory?

text:
Australian Perspective 
The delegation was led by Prime Minister Billy Hughes.   During the war, there was great 
popular support for Australia's involvement in the war, it was not universal. In particular, the 
issue of conscription created great debate in the Australian community. Australian troops 
fighting overseas enlisted voluntarily and at first there was great enthusiasm for enlistment. 
However, the huge toll of deaths and the length of the war meant that by 1916 the number of 
volunteers was not sufficient to meet the requirements of the British military command. 
Australian soldiers fought in Turkey, Belgium and France. Australian involvement in World 
War I is synonymous with the legend of the Anzacs (ANZAC = Australian and New Zealand 
Army Corps). The name became famous with the landing of the Corps on the Gallipoli 
Peninsula, Turkey on 25 April 1915. It was the first military engagement in which significant 
numbers of Australians fought and died as Australian nationals. The Anzacs were part of an 
Allied campaign against the Turks to control the Dardanelles  (the straits that connect the 
Black Sea and the Mediterranean Sea) and thus open the way to Constantinople and Eastern 
Europe. The Gallipoli campaign resulted in the deaths of 7,600 Australians and 2,500 New 
Zealanders and the wounding of 19,000 Australians and 5,000 New Zealanders. Despite the 
defeat, the legend attached to the heroism, comradeship and valour of the soldiers, 
stretcher-bearers, medical officers and others involved remains a source of Australian pride 
and national identity. More than 60,000 Australians were killed during the war. By 1920, 
about 90,000 Australian ex-servicemen were living with a permanent disability.  This was a 
disproportionately high number of casualties for Australia’s population. Australia’s 60,000 
official war dead represented 1.2 per cent of Australia’s people compared to America’s 
117,000 casualties (0.1 per cent of its population). Prisoners of war included 4,044 of whom 
397 died while captive.   
 
The Australian delegation wanted war reparations, annexation of German New Guinea 
and the rejection of the Japanese racial equality proposal. Japan proposed including a “racial 
equality clause” to the Covenant of the League of Nations which stated, “the equality of 
nations being a basic principle of the League of Nations, the High Contracting Parties agree 
to accord as soon as possible to all alien nationals of states, members of the League, equal 
and just treatment in every respect making no distinction, either in law or in fact, on account 
of their race or nationality.” Australia lobbied Great Britain to defend Australia’s “White 
Australia Policy,” resulting in Japan turning away from the west and pursuing a more militant 
nationalism. Hughes did obtain a class C mandate for New Guinea.   The Mandate system 
was created by the Big Four within the League of Nations before the Treaty of Versailles was 
even signed.  This was an attempt to stop the cycle of war and fighting over conquered land 
of the Ottomans and the Germans by giving away it to the winners of the war so that “these 
responsible nations” could manage them and they might gradually develop and mature to 
earn independence.  Some nations were close to being able to govern themselves (Class A 
Mandates like Palestine, Jordan, Iraq, Lebanon and Syria, others at medium stages (Class B:  
Kamerun, Tanganyika and others with no hope soon of self- determination (Class C: New 
Guinea, Nauru, SW Africa..) President Wilson was offended by Australian territorial 
demands and questioned their motivation in profiting off of Germany’s defeat in order to 
extend its sovereignty as far north of the equator.      
 
HINTS: 
1.​ Australia’s White Australia policy is important to understanding why they were so 
against the Racial Equality Clause.

text:
Romania: Queen Marie   
  
Before joining World War I, Queen Marie (a Princess at the beginning of the war) urged the 
government to join the Entente. On August 16, 1916, Romania declared war against 
Austria-Hungary. Three months later, Romania’s capital, Bucharest, was taken over by the 
Central Powers. Unexpected events during the war, forced Romania to sign an armistice with 
the Central Powers. However, this treaty would not be signed by the King of Romania and 
did not take effect. Romania rejoined the war on Entente side (again) one day before the war 
ended. During the beginning stages of the Paris Peace Conference, Romania pushed for the 
independence of Romania. However, Romania was not treated fairly since they were seen as 
a country who switched sides during the war.  
 
Queen Marie privately traveled to Paris where she convinced many world leaders 
into treating Romania fairly. Although her actions were helpful for Romania, the country did 
not get the war reparations they wanted. Romania refused to sign the Treaty of Versailles 
until changes were made in favor of Romania. Not getting what they wanted, the Romanian 
government resigned. A newly formed government signed the Treaty. Romania never got the 
land they wanted after the war.   
  
●​ Hint: Look at the aftermath of the treaty between Hungary and Romania.   
●​ Hint: Look up the Alliance Treaty of 1916 between Romania, UK, France, Russia, 
and Italy. See how later actions from Romania hurt this treaty and made Romania 
seem to be an untrustworthy country.   
●​ Hint: Look at how Russia’s actions toward the end of WWI played a major impact on 
the actions taken by Romania. (Key Word: Bolshevik Revolution)

text:
Ho Chi Minh - Vietnam 
Born to a poor country scholar in the village of Kim Lien, Vietnam, Ho Chi Minh found his 
way to social activism as lowly paid worker in France. At the conclusion of World War 1, he 
led a delegation of Vietnamese living in France and addressed an eight-point petition to the 
representatives of the great powers at the Versailles Peace Conference. The petition sought: 
 
1.     General amnesty for natives who had been condemned for political activity. 
 
2.     Reform of Indochinese justice by granting natives similar judicial privileges as the 
Europeans. 
 
3.     Freedom of press and speech. 
 
4.     Freedom of association and assembly. 
 
5.     Freedom to emigrate and to travel abroad. 
 
6.     Freedom of education, and creation of technical schools for the native population. 
 
7.     Replacement of regime with random rules by regime of law. 
 
8.     A permanent delegation of native people elected to attend French parliament and 
represent needs of the natives. 
 
His proposals would not have meant independence for Vietnam, but instead called for greater 
equity, more basic freedoms, and Vietnamese representation in the colonial government. This 
act brought no response from the peacemakers, but it made him a hero to many politically 
conscious Vietnamese.

text:
Jan Smuts – South Africa  
Born in 1870 in South Africa ( then a British colony) Smuts was educated in England. During 
World War I he rejoined the South African army and led them into battles against the 
Germans in East Africa. He did work with the English in 1917 as a strategist in the war 
against Germany. At Versailles, he was the representative for South Africa and was an 
advocate ( supported) for reconciliation with Germany. However, he did believe that 
Germany was responsible for monetary damages. He was a supporter of U.S. President 
Woodrow Wilson and his idea of “peace without victory”. He supported the idea of the 14 
points and also was in favor of the “mandate” system where the League of Nations would 
take charge of Germany’s overseas possessions after the war. 
HINT: It is important to understand the complexity of the opinions that Smuts held- he 
supported Wilson and the League of Nations but was concerned about US power; he agreed 
with German reparations but also felt reconciliation was important; he wanted a South 
African voice at the table but did not support colored or black rights in South Africa.

text:
Indian delegation 
India was given representation at the Treaty of Versailles even though it was not politically 
free from Great Britain. This was important as no other country that was not autonomous (not 
controlled by another country) was given this right. Montagu and Singh were also included in 
the Indian delegation to the Paris Peace Conference of 1919. Also included as technical 
advisers were: Arthur Hirtzel, Assistant Under-Secretary of State for India; J. Dunlop Smith, 
Political Officer of the India Office; and L. Kershaw, Secretary to the Financial and Statistical 
Section of the India Office.  
 
The Indian plenipotentiaries signed the peace treaties alongside representatives of other 
sovereign states on the basis of legal equality of status. As a signatory of the Treaty of 
Versailles, India was granted automatic entry to the League of Nations. India’s delegation 
supported the Treaty and Wilson’s 14 points and was the only colony to be included in the 
League of Nations that was not self-governing. Gandhi was supportive of the newly created 
Indian National Congress who were not allowed to be represented at Versailles as they were 
asking for freedom to create their own government not under Great Britain’s control. Gandhi 
was very frustrated by this and as a result, began a series of non-violent protests to rid India 
of Great Britain’s occupation. 
 
Hints: 
1.​ Why would India feel that they deserved self-determination?  What was their role in 
the war? 
2.​ Be able to articulate how it must have seemed hypocritical that France and the US did 
not apply the same values towards overseas colonies, as they implemented in their 
own nations. Don’t the values of self-determination (Wilson) and Liberté, égalité, 
fraternité, French for "liberty, equality, fraternity", [ the national motto of France] 
apply to the Indians and all colonized peoples? 
3.​ What was the Amritsar Massacre that occurred in April 1919 and how would this 
change Gandhi’s demands and attitudes towards the British?

text:
Ottoman Empire (later the Republic of Turkey) - Kemal Mustafa  
(Ataturk)  
Kemal was a highly intelligent, brave and charismatic leader. He fought in the front lines 
during the first world war and successfully held off the Australian, New Zealand and British 
forces from taking the Ottoman capital Constantinople (Istanbul).  After the defeat of the 
enemies who attacked his country, he erected a memorial to honor them with these words 
inscribed on it: 
“Those heroes that shed their blood and lost their lives ... You are now lying in the soil of a 
friendly country. Therefore rest in peace. There is no difference between the Johnnies 
[British] and the Mehmets [Turkish] to us where they lie side by side here in this country of 
ours ... You, the mothers who sent their sons from faraway countries, wipe away your tears; 
your sons are now lying in our bosom and are in peace. After having lost their lives on this 
land they have become our sons as well.” 
After WWI, disgusted by the weak leadership of Turkish politicians, Kemal led Turkish 
forces against invading Greek, Italian and French forces, ultimately winning and forcing them 
to sign a new treaty in 1923, which established modern Turkey. After this the Turkish people 
began calling him ‘Ataturk’: the father of the Turks. 
Hint: Read the above quote from Kemal Mustafa – what words would you use to describe 
him? 
Hint: How might Kemal Mustafa react to Europeans’ mainstream anti-Islamic prejudices?

text:
Middle East: T.E. Lawrence 
  
Before joining World War I, the Arab states had been promised independence from Great 
Britain if they helped fight against the Ottoman Empire, an ally of Germany. One of the 
British officers, T.E. Lawrence, encouraged the Arabs to revolt against the Ottomans. 
Fighting alongside the Arabs during the war, TE Lawrence pushed for Arab independence 
during the Paris Peace Conference. However, a secret agreement between Great Britain and 
France said that France would control Syria if the Ottoman Empire fell. Great Britain and 
France carved up the Middle East. Syria, Lebanon, and Turkish Cilicia were given to France. 
Britain gained Iraq, Palestine, and Jordan. Fighting for the Arabs, TE Lawrence was only able 
to help keep the leaders on the thrones for Iraq and Jordan. In the end, the Arab point of view 
was mostly ignored. 
  
Hint: Look at the relationship between the Arabs’ pleas and the American responses. 
Hint: Research how this impacted the region in the future. 
Hint: Research the role of Prince Feisal at the Paris Peace Conference.

text:
Zionist Perspective 
A delegation of the Zionist Organization led by Chaim Weizmann presents the case for a 
Jewish homeland in Palestine to the Paris Peace Conference at the conclusion of World War I. 
 The statement, which included suggested boundaries, proposed that the newly established 
British Mandate should promote Jewish immigration and settlement, encourage 
self-government and ensure religious freedoms. The British had already made it clear that 
they supported a new Jewish state with the Balfour Declaration in 1916.  In response to the 
decisions by the international community before and during the conference, Arabs who had 
no say in what happened at the conference or in how the former Ottoman territory was carved 
up and divided by the French and the British. The Mandate system was created by the Big 
Four within the League of Nations before the Treaty of Versailles was even signed.  This was 
an attempt to stop the cycle of war and fighting over conquered land of the Ottomans and the 
Germans by giving away it to the winners of the war so that “these responsible nations” could 
manage them and they might gradually develop and mature to earn independence.  Some 
nations were close to being able to govern themselves (Class A Mandates like Palestine,

text:
Blaise Diagne (Haitian) – Pan-Africanist 
As the first African elected to the French National Assembly and hold a political post in The 
French government, Blaise often criticized oppression and discrimination of the black 
population in the colonies right at the start of his career as a customs agent in France. As the 
Versailles Peace Treaty deliberations were in progress, Diagne and other Pan-Africanists with 
funding from American Civil Rights and other organizations like the NACCP convened a Pan 
African Congress.  
With an attendance record of approximately sixty representatives from sixteen nations, 
protectorates, and colonies, the congress attracted delegates with little, if any, first-hand 
knowledge of the African continent.  Conference participants adopted a resolution calling for 
the drafting of a code of law “for the international protection of the natives of Africa.” While 
congress attendees insisted that African natives should be allowed eventually to participate in 
their own government, they did not demand African self-determination. Despite the moderate 
nature of the demands, the European and American powers represented at the Versailles 
Peace Conference remained noncommittal. 
HINT: Black Representatives from the Caribbean, North America and Africa all are 
proponents of these ideas.  
HINT: Be sure to address the idea of self-determination.   
HINT: Some of the Africans will address ideas of Negritude and Pan-Africanism.  What does 
this mean and why is it significant?

text:
Brazil - Epitacio de Silva Pessoa 
Brazil was eager to expand it’s economy to take advantage of gaps in the world trade left by 
Europe during WWI. Ignoring German warnings, putting profit before the lives of its people, 
Brazil traded with countries at war with Germany and subsequently lost many merchant ships 
to German U-boat attacks. After the USA declared war on Germany it seemed almost 
inevitable that Germany would lose. Keen to reap the rewards of victory, desperate to join the 
war before it was over, Brazil quickly changed its near pacifist constitution.  Using the 
Germany U-boat attacks as an official justification Brazil joined WWI on October 26, 1917.  
A Brazilian official declared that this war was necessary as they were fighting for “… [a] 
better world … liberty…lasting peace … equal rights … justice and equity.” This was more 
as a declaration for support of the USA, as it imitated Wilson’s own feelings, than any real 
shift in Brazilian foreign policy. The fact that Brazil only sent one medical unit and some 
airmen demonstrates that.  Its “participation” in the war was rewarded with a seat at the 
post-war bargaining table (as a ‘Versailles ally’ of economically powerful USA).   Epitacio de 
Silva Pessoa was not Brazil’s first choice to represent them at Versailles, however the original 
man did not want the job. He was also not a man of the Brazilian people, instead he was more 
interested in looking after the interests of the powerful, corrupt and rich of Brazil. During 
WWI, with Europe distracted by the fighting, Brazil’s industries had done well – however 
with the war over the Brazilian economy was again starting to suffer and so needed loans 
from the USA. Subsequently, he fully supported the aims of the USA at Versailles. 
Hint: Why would Brazil be so keen to want to impress the USA? 
Hint: What would Brazil’s main objectives be at Versailles (global liberty or money?) 
Hint: What dangers might Brazil face now that European countries was no longer fighting 
each other?

text:
Korean Perspective 
 
Korea at the time was a colony of the Japanese, a status that had been recognized by the 
Americans in 1905, in return for Japanese recognition of the Philippines as an American 
colony. President Wilson’s called for “self-determination” led the Koreans to believe that this 
notion applied to them and with the beginning of the Paris Peace talks, on March 1st, 1919 the 
Koreans planned a peaceful march protesting Japanese rule. The move was made largely by 
Korea's teachers, Christian pastors and professional men. Participants in the demonstration 
were asked to carry homemade flags and to chant "may Korea live a thousand years." It was a 
day that was to become a great day of remembrance and mourning. The march was about 
500,000 strong and witnessed by some American citizens. Japan's agents in Korea labeled the 
demonstrations as riots. Troops fired into the demonstrators. Japanese forces attacked and 
burned Christian churches. 6,670 Koreans died, 14,611 were wounded, and 52,770 arrested.  
Protestors were arrested, jailed and tortured for standing up for Korean independence having 
taken Wilson at his word.  The Japanese would not permit a delegation to travel to Paris, 
however three unofficial representatives, including Kim Gyu-sik, a Korean nationalist and 
secretly, the Korean government in exile’s foreign minister, were there posing as YMCA 
delegates. They gained a meeting with one of the Americans, giving him the “Petition of the 
Korean People and Nation for Liberation from Japan and for the Reconstitution of Korea as 
an Independent State” and the “Claims of the Korean People and Nation.”  The concerns 
raised, namely, the desire for Korean independence, were never brought to President Wilson, 
and little came of their visit.  Before leaving he gave a speech which asked whether Woodrow 
Wilson meant what he said about self-determination and criticized the French who pretended 
to love justice but cared little about 20 million Koreans suffering under Japanese colonial 
oppression which included censorship and forced rice exports to Japan, leaving their own 
people hungry. Kim would later become a Communist and describe the hypocrisy of the 
Americans. 
 
HINTS: 
1.​ Emphasize Korean nationalism, but this is not just a desire for independence but a 
desire to help the well-being of the Korean people—they have been oppressed by a 
cruel occupier, gone hungry in order to fill the bellies of the Japanese, and have been 
unable to protest even peacefully.   Read the link which contains Young Park’s 
Manifesto.  Great language to use here! 
2.​ You will want to talk about how the Americans and the French are hypocritical.  Why 
don’t the values of self-determination (Wilson) and Liberté, égalité, fraternité, French 
for "liberty, equality, fraternity", [ the national motto of France] apply to the Koreans?

Zionist Perspective 
A delegation of the Zionist Organization led by Chaim Weizmann presents the case for a 
Jewish homeland in Palestine to the Paris Peace Conference at the conclusion of World War I. 
 The statement, which included suggested boundaries, proposed that the newly established 
British Mandate should promote Jewish immigration and settlement, encourage 
self-government and ensure religious freedoms. The British had already made it clear that 
they supported a new Jewish state with the Balfour Declaration in 1916.  In response to the 
decisions by the international community before and during the conference, Arabs who had 
no say in what happened at the conference or in how the former Ottoman territory was carved 
up and divided by the French and the British. The Mandate system was created by the Big 
Four within the League of Nations before the Treaty of Versailles was even signed.  This was 
an attempt to stop the cycle of war and fighting over conquered land of the Ottomans and the 
Germans by giving away it to the winners of the war so that “these responsible nations” could 
manage them and they might gradually develop and mature to earn independence.  Some 
nations were close to being able to govern themselves (Class A Mandates like Palestine, 
Jordan, Iraq, Lebanon and Syria, others at medium stages (Class B:  Kamerun, Tanganyika 
and others with no hope of self- determination (Class C: New Guinea, Nauru, SW Africa..)

in 1948, further dislocating Palestinians throughout the region.

TRENCH RATS
One soldier described ﬁnding a group of dead bodies while on patrol: "I saw some 
rats running from under the dead men's greatcoats, enormous rats, fat with human 
ﬂesh. My heart pounded as we edged towards one of the bodies. His helmet had 
rolled oﬀ. The man displayed a grimacing face, stripped of ﬂesh; the skull bare, the 
eyes devoured and from the yawning mouth leapt a rat.“
 "Rats came up from the canal, fed on the plentiful corpses, and multiplied 
exceedingly. While I stayed here with the Welch, a new oﬃcer joined the company 
and, in token of welcome, was given a dug-out containing a spring-bed. When he 
turned in that night he heard a scuﬄing, shone his torch on the bed, and found two 
rats on his blanket tussling for the possession of a severed hand."
title: Trench rats — soldier accounts

text:
TRENCH FOOT 
●
“If you have never had trench foot described to you, I will explain. Your feet swell to two to 
three times their normal size and go completely dead. You can stick a bayonet into them 
and not feel a thing. If you are lucky enough not to lose your feet and the swelling starts to 
go down, it is then that the most indescribable agony begins. I have heard men cry and 
scream with pain and many have had to have their feet and legs amputated. I was one of 
the lucky ones, but one more day in that trench and it may have been too late.”
